tourists annually. It owes its attractiveness to: French cuisine; viticulture areas; numerous festivals; and historic Renaissance Gothic 
buildings listed by UNESCO (Insse, 2021; Vidal, 2017; Mallea et al., 2018; Vannucci et al., 2019; BTC, 2021). The agricultural area of 
approximately 112,000 ha, with 9000 unique growers, produces more than 700 million bottles of wine annually. 
As of the year 2007, the City of Bordeaux had a total of 350 buildings registered by UNESCO (BTC, 2021). This study includes an 
analysis of two of these historic buildings, Grosse Cloche (clock area) (Fig. 2(A)) and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e (Fig. 2(C)), which were built 
in the 4th century CE and later rebuilt in the 11th century CE. These two buildings feature Romanesque architecture, a 14th century 
Gothic choir loft, three beautiful portals, funerary wall paintings, Nottingham alabaster, bas-reliefs and 18th century railings make the 
cathedral a testimony of a thousand years of port city history from Bordeaux. The 19th century was marked by several restorations of 
Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e. More than 1 million Euros were invested in restoration projects in 1995 alone (Gallet, 2017). 
For this reason, in addition to the cultural importance of the sites, self-made passive samplers (SMPSs) were installed with extreme care 
in an effort not to compromise or damage the external walls of the historic buildings (Fig. 2(B)). 
The restoration of these sites stimulated increased touristic activity in the central region of the port city of Bordeaux. Boivin and 
Tanguay (2019) state that many tourists prefer to visit monuments located in public urban spaces. This plays an essential role in the 
attractiveness of Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e (BTC, 2021). Consequently, these sites’ restoration activities increase the 
attractiveness of tourism focused on the perspective of local sustainability, generating work and income for the local population 
(Ahmad et al., 2019). These development strategies make it possible to increase the reach of the city and, at the same time, guarantee 
the sustainability of the tourism industry (Demir et al., 2020). Furthermore, the integration of tourist considerations in relation to the 
formation of urban public policies has the potential to offer efficient services to reduce air pollution in order to further stimulate the 
interest of visitors in cities (Boivin and Tanguay, 2019; D’arco et al., 2021). 
Both Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e have been shown to accumulate black crusts on their external façades. This formation 
is caused by several environmental factors, namely: shade, humidity, temperature, low sunlight, as well as the presence of atmospheric 
contaminants (Comite et al., 2020; Samara et al., 2020; Morillas et al., 2020; Oliveira et al., 2021a, 2021b). Additionally, the formation 
of black crusts is highlightedby Oliveira et al. (2021a, 2021b), to be one of the main causes of the degradation of historic buildings and 
structures caused by the accumulation of the concentration of atmospheric pollutants. Fig. 3 records our documentation of the 
accumulation of black crusts, in the following architectural elements of the historic buildings studied: Pinnacle (A), Rose window (B), 
Arcade (C) and Archivolt (D).

2021). Many of the contaminants contatined within this polluted air later settle onto the surfaces of historic buildings (Ramírez et al., 
2020; Saini et al., 2020; Oliveira et al., 2021a; Brodny and Tutak, 2021). This, according to Rajput et al. (2020), results in increased 
rates of degradation of historic structures through corrosion. The accumulation of ultrafine particles (UFPs) and nanoparticles (NPs) on 
the external areas of historic buildings can directly and negatively interfere both in the structural integrity of buildings and cause a 
decline in human health as visitors and residents inhale these particles (Rajput et al., 2020). Therefore, this release of UFPs and NPs 
into the atmosphere becomes a consequence of economic development. While local communities may enjoy a stimulated economy, 
increased tourism in general contributes ironically to the degradation of many of the historic buildings the tourists are coming to see. 
Risks are also posed to the local population’s health through increased exposure to airborne pollutants (Silva et al., 2020a; Oliveira 
et al., 2021a). 
The elements present in UFPs and NPs, commonly found in atmospheric contamination, may contain highly dangerous elements 
such as arsenic (As), mercury (Hg), cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb), in addition to numerous potential carcinogenic organic phases 
(Howard et al., 2019; Zahmatkesh et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021). Liu et al. (2019), highlights the reality of high levels of air pollution in 
modern day China and India, which exhibit excessive CO2 (carbon dioxide), CH4 (methane) and N2O (nitrous oxide) in the atmosphere. 
According to Herrera and Videla (2009), research related to surface contamination on historic buildings in relation to their state of 
deterioration is justified within the international scientific community. They suggest research projects that analyze and focus on the 
real effects of atmospheric contaminants and their consequences on these historic buildings. Of special note is the impact wrought on 
metallic structures due to oxidation and the degeneration of paint pigments used in historic buildings (Oliveira et al., 2021a). 
It is important to remember that cultural and historical buildings degrade more quickly when located in dense urban areas due to 
the accumulation of UFPs and NPs on their surfaces (Suzuki et al., 2018). According to some studies, the impacts of atmospheric 
pollution, due to the presence of toxic particles, acts not only as an agent of degradation of historical and cultural buildings, but can 
directly compromise the well-being and health of the local population (Silva et al., 2020a; Oliveira et al., 2021b). According to Gallego- 
Cartagena et al. (2020) and Comite et al. (2020), the solution for the preservation of historic buildings exposed to atmospheric 
contamination is future projects aimed at their restoration. 
In France, according to Audurier-Cros (1982), increases in air pollution recorded in 1980 in both industrial and urban areas of port 
regions resulted from the unloading of oil from ships, and later, the consumption of fossil fuel on a regional scale. Bentayeb et al. 
(2014) found a high presence of particulate material (PM10), nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and Ozone (O3) when estimating levels of 
dangerous elements derived from atmospheric contamination in some French regions from 1989 to 2008. 
According to Quimbayo-Duarte et al. (2021), France currently registers high levels of atmospheric pollution in its urbanized areas, 
before the Covid pandemic, resulting from sources of industrial and urban emissions. These emissions release hazardous elements in 
gaseous form into the atmosphere, causing harmful impacts to the health of the French population. As Omrani et al. (2020) report, 
France needs to contemplate monitoring actions in relation to air quality with the creation of public policies that can assess and 
mitigate the impacts of air pollution in an incisive and immediate way. 
The objects of this study are Grosse Cloche and the Cath´edrale St-Andr´e, located in the port city of Bourdeaux, in the southwest of 
France. The City of Bourdeaux is located in one of the most important viticulture areas in the world. Wines produced in this region 
stand out for presenting high levels of quality compared to wines produced elsewhere (BTC, 2021). According to Zamberlan et al. 
(2020), agricultural production can contribute to the quantity of atmospheric pollution through the use of fungicides that contain Cu 
(copper) and Ca (calcium) sulfates, which have a high influence on atmospheric contamination. In this case, in the port city of 
Bourdeaux, located in close proximity to the agricultural activities of wine production, diminished air quality and petroleum-based 
residues could be increasing the degradation of historic buildings, together with emissions from vehicular traffic, airport opera­
tions, and port logistics. 
The choice of our research objects (Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e) is justified due to their historical importance as listed 
cultural sites by UNESCO, exhibiting architectural details in a medieval Gothic Renaissance style, originated from the Germanic 
barbarian people who conquered and occupied modern-day northern France from 1050 to 1100 CE (Vidal, 2017; Mallea et al., 2018; 
Vannucci et al., 2019). Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e are considered to be among the most important historical and cultural 
heritage sites not only in Europe, but among the most significant of humanity. Their design, however, concentrate structural problems 
and lead to infiltration. 
The general objective of this study is to analyze the presence of dangerous elements in the external structures of Grosse Cloche and 
Cath´edrale St-Andr´e due to the influence of atmospheric pollutants. Studies involving the presence of atmospheric nanoparticles in 
historic buildings, according to Silva et al. (2020a) and Oliveira et al. (2021a, 2021b) become extremely important for the preservation 
of historic buildings listed by humanity. This study stands out for the importance of studying two historic buildings in France, in 
relation to the identification of chemical elements originating from atmospheric pollution, which act as a degradation agent in these 
buildings, enhancing the creation of new public policies, aimed at preserving the historic heritage. What favors the emergence and 
foundation for future studies, since the method used in this study, according to Oliveira et al. (2021a, 2021b) is the only and most 
innovative that exists for the assessment of the degradation of historic buildings by atmospheric contaminants on a global scale.

Additionally, in the present study, it is noted that many UFPs were found around pores (Fig. 4). This shows that the pores cannot be 
considered as adsorbents of ultra-thin material, as in most cases it was detected that UFPs were only “temporarily” hosted in the pores. 
It is worth mentioning that the samples collected with SMPSs contained many carbonaceous particles, indicating that these spheres 
are composed of organometallic formations. In the samples collected on the exterior walls of the cathedral, in contrast, the occurrence 
of totally inorganic spheres prevailed. In this context, the presence of metallic particles in the samples collected with SMPSs may be 
related to the presence of the train station located in the vicinity of the historic buildings of Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e. 
Although urban trains are a cleaner means of transport, according to several authors, this mode of transport (trains) can also release 
particles harmful to human health and buildings (Pietrzak and Pietrzak, 2019; Al-Thawadi et al., 2020; Yan-Zhe et al., 2021). In this 
present study, many metallic particles composed of Ti, Cr, Fe, Sb, Mo and major elements such as: Al, Si, Ca, K and Na were detected. 
These likely derive from the wear of the train’s brakes and tracks and were later combined with soil and the sedimented dust of 
construction material. When particles with similar composition are not detected in the other points, points distant from the train 
tracks, it is assumed that this means of transport emits metallic particles containing elements toxic to human health. This is more likely 
when compared to other possible sources, such as soil and/or degradation of construction material. If the latter was indeed the source, 
all samples would have yielded particles of similar composition regardless of their proximity to the tracks. 
Lima et al. (2021) highlight the predominance of several toxic elements (e.g. Pb, Cr, Cd, Fe, V, Hg, Ba, Zn, Ni, and Sn) in high 
concentrations in NPs when collecting samples on train station platforms. Thus, they suggest protective measures be implemented in 
order to safeguard the health of employees and passengers who have a daily need to use the train. This fact is not of concern to tourists, 
given that the exposure time is not as long as it is for people who live and work in that region. Thus, it is recommended that local 
authorities evaluate measures to mitigate such an impact. Examples include either washing the streets frequently or requiring the train 
company to utilize brake pads that do not contain potentially toxic elements. Additionally, “green curtains” composed of vegetation 
that absorb particulate material derived from trains can be established and maintained near railroad cooridors. Neckel et al. (2020) 
highlight that public policies should encourage projects that include urban vegetation as they not onlycontribute to positive air quality, 
they also provide urban thermal comfort and enhance the quality of life of the local population. 
In the samples obtained by SMPSs, the particles that are suspected of being derived from trains do not contain K, Ca, and Na. It is 
therefore believed that such elements form more dense particles that avoid being re-suspended after they settle. Fig. 5 demonstrates 
this statement by means of a classic EDS of the studied samples, composed of plaster, amorphous phases of concrete, quartz and clay, 
where the presence of chemical elements was detected. 
Between 10 and 45 amorphous copper sulfate particles were detected in each of the samples. Thus, it is surmised that there is a high 
probibility that copper sulfate fungicide (CuSO4) drift is being contributed by the agricultural areas of wine production to the center of 
the City of Bourdeaux. This represents a high risk to people’s health, as CuSO4 is highly toxic (Zamberlan et al., 2020). Chen et al. 
(2020) and Hamza et al. (2021), point out that CuSO4 is generally released to the environment by agricultural and industrial activities. 
This contamination may cause health problems, disturbing the well-being of the local population. 
Numerous clusters of nanoparticles between 5 and 97 nm were detected. EDS analysis showed that they basically contained Cu, Ca, 
S, and O (Fig. 6). This leads us to suspect that the local cultivation of grapes and resultant use of fungicides containing sulfates of Cu 
and Ca have a high influence on the atmospheric contamination of the City of Bourdeaux. Therefore, in addition to vehicular traffic, the 
port, and industrial activity, agriculture plays a significant role in the atmospheric contamination in this region. This result is of much 
larger, global interest as copper sulfates are regularly used as fungicides for the cultivation of grapes, apples, oranges and many other 
crops in Brazil, China, the United States and many other countries. 
In both samples obtained with SMPSs and the sedimented dust, organic NPs associated with the metallic particles that are hy­
pothesized to be sourced from trains were detected. This can be inferred as the presence of carbonaceous matter from sources such as

detected in the samples collected in this study both via SMPS and in sedimented dust. Even in the presence of carbonaceous material, 
this mineral occurred as an adsorbent of toxic elements, which indicates that it can also act as a potent immobilizer of such elements. 
Goethite was the only iron hydroxide that always contained dangerous elements. Although goethite can present risks to human 
health, in agricultural activities it reduces oxidation stress, contributing to plant growth (Irshad et al., 2020). This agricultural use must 
be taken into account due to Bourdeaux’s prevalance of vineyards. The analyses detected 39 goethite particles, 31 of which were in the 
SMPS samples and only 8 were found in the sedimented dust (Fig. 7A). When in the presence of agglomerated Fe and Al amorphous 
phases, the geothite nanoparticles contained As, Cd, Hg, Pb (Fig. 7B). However, when detected as an isolated crystal it contained only 
As and Hg. This indicates that the amorphous phases combined with this hydroxide help in the adsorption of toxic elements. The oxide 
most frequently detected after quartz was hematite (Fig. 7C). The particles of this mineral were more abundant in sedimented dust than 
in SMPS samples. It is believed that this is due to the fact that it is a dense mineral and that it is hardly suspended in particulate matter. 
Hematite, although it may be of mineral origin, can also be formed from the dehydration of goethite emitted by anthropogenic sources, 
which demonstrates the complexity when evaluating NPs in the areas of Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e. 
In this study, more than 800 organic NPs containing high levels of toxic elements were detected. Of these, 78% were detected in 
samples obtained via SMPSs and the others in sedimented dust. This is likely due to the fact that they are less dense particles than the 
detected minerals, which facilitates their suspension and re-suspension in the atmosphere of the studied region. Among these particles, 
more than 60% presented with a diameter of less than 50 nm, which results in greater concern as particles of this size can easily pass 
through the respiratory system into the bloodstream, generating greater impacts on human health. In addition, no organic particles 
were detected that were totally crystalline or amorphous, all NPs contained multiple degrees of crystallinity (Fig. 7E), and 579 
contained elements such as As, Cr, Fe, Pb in addition to major elements such as Al, Ca, K, and Si. 
Although 382 sulfate NPs were detected, jarosite (Fig. 7D) was the sulfate that was most studied in this work as it is extremely 
acidic. The jarosite (KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6) samples analyzed in this study also contained high proportions of the toxic elements: As, Cd, Cr, 
Hg, Mo, Pb, Se, and Zn. Therefore, being a water-soluble salt in the presence of moisture and rainwater, it can dissolve and mobilize the 
toxic elements found in its crystalline structure (Trueman et al., 2021). This has the potential to generate high impacts on the health of 
people living in the City of Bourdeaux, in addition to leading to enhanced degradation of construction materials. Jarosite was also 
detected in different sizes, varying between 43 nm and 5 μm. NPs present a greater risk as they have a larger surface area and are more 
reactive than larger particles. 
The sedimented dust samples obtained at Cath´edrale St-Andr´e (A) and in the Grosse Cloche area (B) (Fig. 8), were very different 
morphologically, in size and chemical composition. In general, the cathedral samples (Fig. 8A), showed particles abundant in minerals, 
while those of the clock also contained many amorphous and organic nanometric particles. In the clock (Fig. 8B), spherical particles 
were all composed of carbonaceous matter, often containing inorganic elements. According to Oliveira et al. (2021a) these inorganic 
elements, when accumulated in the external structure of buildings, degrade their structure. This presents an important challenge for 
restoration activities in these historic structures. 
The results of this study demonstrate the contamination of NPs and UFPs with the presence of potentially toxic inorganic elements, 
which contribute to the degradation of the historic buildings of Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e. It is the suggestion of the 
authors to carry out constant restoration activities in order to preserve the structures studied (Suzuki et al., 2018; Comite et al., 2020; 
Gallego-Cartagena et al., 2020; Hatđr, 2020; Oliveira et al., 2021a, 2021b). 
The carbonaceous materials and organic acids identified in the samples collected in this study enhance the weathering of the 
historic, UNESCO listed buildings analyzed, in addition to accumulating chemical elements that can be dangerous to human health. 
These contaminants originated from atmospheric contamination sourced from a combination of vehicular traffic, public transit sys­
tems and the agricultural activities of the region’s wineries. Through these results, and with the understanding of the sources of 
pollution, it is possible according to Hatđr (2020), to build and design urban policies that will preserve historic buildings like Grosse 
Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e, not only in the port city of Bourdeaux, but in all areas of the planet where similar human activities and 
pollution exist. 
4. Conclusion 
Although there is regular vehicular traffic in both areas studied, not all samples of SMPSs had a high proportion of organic particles 
in all size fractions analyzed. At the Cath´edrale St-Andr´e, the samples had lower proportions of carbonaceous particles, likely due to 
the fact that it is located in an area with greater natural ventilation, more trees and with lower overall vehicular traffic. Higher speed 
limits and fewer vehicular delays also speed commuters’ travel near the cathedral. An important factor that favors the high proportion 
of carbonaceous matter in the Grosse Cloche area is the occurrence of a corridor that facilitates an increase in vehicular traffic, in 
addition to the aforementioned fact that they remain stationary longer and/or travel slower in this area as opposed to the cathedral 
area. 
The collected sedimented dust contained high proportions of organometalic particles containing: Al, As, Ba, Ca, Cd, Co, Cr, Fe, K, 
Mg, Mn, Mo, Na, Ni, Pb, S, Sb, Se, Si, Sn, Ti, V, and Zn. When evaluating the collected particles with EDS and elementary mapping, it 
was possible to confirm that, unlike Grosse Cloche, at Cath´edrale St-Andr´e the particles that contained Ni and V were less abundant and 
were isolated; that is, without agglomerations with major elements derived from the soil and construction material. This indicates that 
they are derived from the combustion of oil and diesel, while on Grosse Cloche the particles were all mixed, indicating an origin 
predominantly from road dust. Furthermore, the particles resulting from oil combustion are agglomerated with major elements. In 
addition, the samples around the cathedral were more inorganic than the clock samples, which had a higher proportion of carbo­
naceous matter.

The port city of Bourdeaux, France has strong urban characteristics which arefocused on tourism and wine production. The 
importance of the historic buildings of Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e, the objects of this study, are in need of constant air 
quality monitoring with periodic restoration activity in order to preserve their invaluable cultural heritage. The authors suggest the 
restoration of the historic structures sampled for the benefit of humanity, in addition to increasing the rigor of public policies to control 
the release of particulate matter, based on the high concentrations of 78%, which were detected in the samples obtained via SMPS and 
the too much in sedimented dust. When considering the results obtained in this study, they can serve as a basis for other researchers to 
monitor and assess the presence of atmospheric pollutants, as possible responsible for the degradation of historic buildings on a global 
scale.

2.2. Analytical methods 
Particulate matter was collected using SMPSs affixed to the external walls of the buildings sampled. Sedimented dusts were 
collected according to Amato et al. (2009), Amato et al. (2011) and Trejos et al. (2021). All samples were collected between June 2018 
and May 2019. In all, 48 samples were collected with the SMPSs and 24 samples of sedimented dust were taken. Samples were collected 
every 3 months from the side walls of Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St -Andr´e, in an effort to retrieve a sample during each of the 4 
seasons (winter, spring, autumn and summer). 
Despite the proximity of the Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e sampling areas, their choice for this study was due to the 
importance of each touristic monument to the city. Also, both are of great cultural and economic importance. The cathedral area is 
more wooded and has a metro station in its direct neighborhood area. For the Grosse Cloche area (characterized by the clock) it was 
decided to affix two SMPSs, one on each side of the street, in the building next to the clock to assess the vehicular traffic corridor in that 
area. In the region of the cathedral, SMPS collectors were allocated at 6 equidistant points around the cathedral. In both objects of 
study, the sedimented dust materials were collected at the same loacations where the SMPSs were located. With this it was possible to 
evaluate the particles suspended at the same average height of the human respiratory system (especially nose and mouth - from 1.61 to 
1.70 m in height) using SMPSs, as well as the material sedimented in the soil which; according to Oliveira et al. (2021b), may become 
re-suspended through normal activities and wind action, and consequently may present a risk to human health and to historic buildings 
in the areas under study. 
It should be noted that SMPSs, when fixed to the walls, also help to understand the dry deposition of particulate material on the 
construction material, which for several authors (Herrera and Videla, 2009; Comite et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2020a; Gallego-Cartagena 
et al., 2020; Oliveira et al., 2021b) directly affect the building’s durability. Also, it should be noted that the collection point on the 
clock is especially important because it is located in a vehicular traffic corridor and because it is next to one of the largest parking lots in 
the city (less than 100 m away). This made it possible to study road dust particles, as well as sedimented material with greater ease and 
precision, when compared to the other sides of the analyzed buildings, which contain less vehicular traffic. 
The collected samples were sent within 24 h for laboratory analysis via collaboration with the University of Bordeaux. Subse­
quently, they were analyzed using electron microscopy techniques, capable of studying the morphology, chemical composition and 
distribution of UFPs and NPs. Particles between 0.1 and 10 μm were analyzed using a Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope 
(FE-SEM) (Silva et al., 2020a; Oliveira et al., 2021a, 2021b); jointly, using the High Resolution Transmission Electron Microscope (HR- 
TEM), which enabled the study of NPs smaller than 100 nm with high resolution. Precisely because it is the most modern technique on 
a global scale for the representation with images of NPs (Xing et al., 2019; Ernould et al., 2020). It was also necessary to couple this 
analysis with an Energy Dispersive X-ray (EDS) microanalysis system, which allowed for a better characterization and identification of 
the analyzed NPs (Brodusch et al., 2020; Hodoroaba, 2020). FE-SEM is gernally used for particles larger than 100 nm. Meanwhile, HR- 
TEM applies better efficacy for particles smaller than 100 nm. 
For a better understanding of the particles that directly impact human health and the historic structures under study, in each sample 
obtained it was decided to analyze: 10 particles between 5 and 10 μm; 30 particles between 1 and 5 μm; and 60 particles between 0.1 
and 1 μm by FE-SEM / EDS. Additionally, 120 particles smaller than 0.1 μm were analyzed as described in previous studies (Silva et al., 
2020a; Oliveira et al., 2021b). As a result, it was possible to maximize the understanding of smaller particles as they represent greater 
dangers to human health and degradation potential in historic buildings (Khajavi et al., 2019; Bessa et al., 2020; Rajput et al., 2020; 
Trejos et al., 2021). 
The road dust sampling procedure followed the process described in several previously published works (Amato et al., 2009, 2011; 
Silva et al., 2020a; Oliveira et al., 2021a). Care was taken not to change the NPs where the particulate matter was sedimented. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Micro-pores, ultra-fine spheres and metallic particles 
High amounts of micro-pores were detected in the collected samples, especially in the sedimented dust samples. The occurrence of 
such pores was mainly due to the wear and tear of the construction material of the historic buildings studied. This effect was also noted 
in previous studies (Silva et al., 2020a; Oliveira et al., 2021a, 2021b). 
According to García-Florentino et al. (2020) atmospheric pollutants become responsible for the corrosive degradation of historic 
buildings, representing a significant cause for concern in the preservation of cultural structures exposed to the open air. In this sense, 
one must take into account the amount of contamination by NPs resulting from air pollution, which, when accumulating on the historic 
building, can generate sulfation reactions. These reactions in turn create new ions, thus modifying the original structure and the 
characteristic of the construction materials. These changes then compromise the durability of historic buildings in regions of moderate 
to high atmospheric pollution (García-Florentino et al., 2020). 
It is believed that the areas sampled at Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e are no different, as they have porous and spherical 
materials in their structure, are exposed to the open air and exist in an urban area of compromised air quality. Such porous particles 
may contain agglomerated NPs composed of dangerous elements, such as: As, Pb, Cd, and Cr. These elements, according to Cao et al. 
(2014) and Neckel et al. (2021), can present very real risks to environmental quality and human health when the population is exposed

3.2. Minerals and semi-amorphous material 
Although magnetite is a mineral and can occur naturally in the environment, it can also be derived from the combustion of diesel 
and gasoline (Neelamegan et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2020b). However, in this study, the mineral magnetite occurred in the presence of

A B S T R A C T  
Urban centers concentrate high levels of atmospheric pollutants, sourced by vehicular traffic, 
public transit systems, industrial emissions and agricultural emissions. This leads to the accu­
mulation of gases and particulate matter (PM) which contribute to the degradation of historic 
buildings. Considering the importance of preserving historic structures, this manuscript examines 
the analysis of dangerous elements on the facades of two historic, UNESCO listed sites in 
Bordeaux, France, Grosse Cloche and Cath´edrale St-Andr´e, due to the multiple influences of at­
mospheric pollutants, responsible for the degradation of historic buildings, in addition to causing 
possible compromises to human health. A total of 48 samples of particulate matter were collected 
between June 2018 and May 2019 using self-made passive samplers (SMPSs). Sedimented dust 
samples were collected from the same locations at the same time, one collection during each of 
the 4 seasons of the year. Analyses of accumulated ultrafine particles (UFPs) and nanoparticles 
(NPs) were performed on the collected samples. The results detected the presence of more than 
800 organic NPs with high levels of toxic elements. Of these, 78% were detected in samples 
obtained via SMPS and the others in sedimented dust. 60% were shown to have a diameter of less 
than 50 nm. The authors suggest restoring the sampled historical structures for the benefit of 
humanity, in addition to increasing the rigor of public policies to control the release of particulate 
matter.
